That is enough to judge whether the method is careful or merely anecdotal. Estimated reading time: 30–45 minutes.52:T45c,The paper presents watermarking in a common formalism. During autoregressive generation, the LLM provides a next-token distribution p_t. A watermark uses pseudorandom vectors U derived from a context hash and a private key, and applies a logits transformation f(U, p_t) to produce a watermarked distribution. Detection recovers token-level scores U_{a_t, token_t} at retained positions, deduplicates repeated seed-token pairs, and relies on those scores being i.i.d. under the null hypothesis. The key addition is a reliability definition with two criteria: soundness in expectation over the private key, and a small probability, for a fixed text distribution, of sampling a key that causes false flags. The autoresearch harness isolates the agent, lets it propose and implement schemes, and submits them to a private verification pipeline. The pipeline first rejects schemes that fail the reliability tests, then evaluates accepted schemes on detectability, robustness, and quality. This structure is designed to prevent agents from winning by raising false-positive rates or overfitting visible evaluation details.53:T710,The work has two technical pieces. First, behavioral auditing. The authors define the Behavioral Necessity Rate (BNR): among instances answered correctly under the full context, remove one annotated evidence target at a time and measure how often the model can no longer recover the answer. This turns the vague notion of “using the intended hop” into an intervention-based behavioral test. To avoid conflating evidence necessity with generic sensitivity to context deletion, they introduce a matched-background control. This is important: a raw accuracy drop after deletion could simply reflect that the example became noisier or shorter in an unfavorable way. The control isolates whether the failure is specific to the claimed evidence.

Second, RealHop, a diagnose-construct-verify framework for rebuilding multi-hop questions so that every step is required. The construction uses three main mechanisms: entity rebinding to break parametric-memory shortcuts and familiar associations; relation splitting / evidence rewriting to force composition across multiple premises rather than allowing a single-step inference; and complete competing paths to alternative answers that look structurally plausible but fail on a required relation, reducing shallow elimination strategies. The authors also separate construction from verification: they freeze the dataset after structural and semantic checks, then run post hoc deletion-based auditing. This avoids overfitting the benchmark to a particular model during creation. For datasets without native hop annotations, such as FRAMES, they reconstruct intervention-ready support units from source-linked evidence. For LongBench v2, they adapt long-context questions into auditable multiple-choice and repeated open-ended protocols to reduce evaluation noise.54:T564,The central empirical finding is that standard multi-hop benchmarks have surprisingly low behavioral necessity. Across MuSiQue, HotpotQA, and 2WikiMultiHopQA, panel-mean BNR is only 16.6% to 27.4%. Even adversarially designed benchmarks intended to reduce shortcuts only reach 43.5% to 48.9%. This means that annotated chains and distractor-heavy construction do not guarantee that correct predictions depend on the intended evidence.

On rebuilt benchmarks, the picture changes sharply. On 790 paired MuSiQue questions, RealHop-MuSiQue raises panel-mean BNR from 27.4% to 94.4%, while full-context accuracy remains in the 68.5% to 83.5% range. That is an important result: the benchmark becomes much more diagnostic without collapsing answerability. On source-linked FRAMES questions, RealHop-FRAMES reaches 88.9% to 89.9% BNR despite the lack of native hop annotations. On 216 long-context questions derived from LongBench v2, the matched multiple-choice protocol expands the accuracy spread across 16 models from 13.9 points to 59.2 points. The wider separation persists under repeated open-ended evaluation, and targeted deletion yields 96.5% to 98.1% BNR for the three audited models. The ablations indicate that no single construction trick is sufficient; entity rebinding, relation splitting, and competing paths each contribute to making every step behaviorally necessary.55:T6cc,The work has three main components. First is a data engine for synthetic long-form conversation. It combines persona- and memory-conditioned dialogue planning, multi-speaker bilingual TTS, and acoustically faithful multi-channel mixing to produce parallel-stream audio with codec-frame-level alignment suitable for Moshi-style training. The important point is that the generator is not just reading text dialogues aloud. It explicitly controls conversation length, number of participants, turn-taking, overlap, backchannels, interruptions, addressee shifts, and long-range coreference, so the training corpus contains the structural patterns that define real multi-party interaction.

Second is MultiTalkBench, an interactive benchmark for end-to-end speech-to-speech systems. It jointly evaluates three axes: long conversations beyond ten minutes with probes for entity tracking and topic coherence, one-model-many-user interaction with metrics for addressee selection and turn-taking, and English-Chinese bilingual ability. This differs from prior long-audio benchmarks, which mostly test passive understanding rather than interactive generation, and from prior speech-to-speech benchmarks, which are usually short and dyadic.

Third is a bilingual Moshi-style full-duplex model trained on the new corpus. The paper stays within the end-to-end unified modeling paradigm rather than reverting to an ASR→LLM→TTS pipeline. For pretraining researchers, the main question is how changing the training distribution changes behavior: with both input and output represented in codec-token space, long context, multi-party interaction, and bilingual switching become part of the language modeling objective itself rather than external modules.56:T469,The strongest asset is the released 57.6k-hour synthetic training corpus, which the authors claim exceeds the combined size of prior open full-duplex speech corpora. When reading the full paper, three result types are worth prioritizing. First, scaling behavior: whether long-context and multi-party abilities improve smoothly with more synthetic data. Second, data-component ablations: what happens when overlap, addressee shifts, memory conditioning, or bilingual mixing are removed. Third, attribution of gains: whether improvements come mainly from corpus scale, richer interaction structure, or model changes. For audio LM work, those are more informative than a single aggregate score.57:T5c2,Xiaomi-OCR-0 is a 0.8B VLM initialized from Qwen3.5-0.8B and trained under a unified image–instruction–response interface. The data contains both region-level samples and page-level samples. Region-level samples pair cropped text, table, or formula regions with recognition targets; page-level samples pair full document images with complete parsing targets, including content, structure, and reading order. The data engine has three components. First, an automated annotation pipeline uses PP-DocLayoutV3 to detect semantic regions, then sends crops to a heterogeneous expert pool. High-agreement labels are accepted; lower-agreement cases go through render-guided correction and re-evaluation; unresolved cases are selectively human-verified. The paper introduces Ensemble Triplet Consensus, which combines pool-wide agreement and agreement within a selected three-expert subset to rank candidate labels. Second, multi-factor sample mining uses expert agreement, model self-consistency, and semantic clustering to shape the training mixture. Third, synthetic generation targets coverage gaps and verified failure modes. The training recipe is progressive: Q-Mask-based text anchoring, multi-task continued pretraining, and Mix-RL on hard examples with verifiable rewards. The paper also compares Mix-RL with multi-teacher on-policy distillation, where distillation is more compute-efficient but longer Mix-RL reaches better final parsing and understanding performance.58:T546,The method has two stages. Stage one is REL-SFT. The authors build a 29.4K Reasoning-Evidence Localization chain-of-thought dataset, where each reasoning trace is aligned with page indices and normalized bounding boxes. Training is done across seven rendering resolutions, so the model learns to localize relevant evidence under compressed global views rather than simply reading everything at high fidelity. Stage two is GRPO. At inference, the model starts from low-DPI page images and iteratively generates a reasoning segment followed by an action: either answer directly or issue a region-enhancement call with a page index and bounding box. A tool then crops the aligned region from a higher-DPI rendering of the same page and returns it as an observation. The model incorporates that observation into subsequent reasoning until it answers or exhausts the call budget. A few design choices matter here: low- and high-resolution views share the same page coordinates, which avoids alignment drift; enhancement is local rather than full-page rerendering, which keeps added visual tokens under control; and policy learning must optimize not only correctness but also when to zoom, where to zoom, and when to stop. The paper also discusses font and point-size selection, highlighting that rendering choices materially affect downstream performance.59:T446,The strongest results are on compressed long-document reasoning. On LongBench, it slightly surpasses its text-input backbone, 56.40 versus 55.86, suggesting that visual compression does not necessarily hurt long-context understanding and may even help through page-level structure plus selective reading. For instance, an I2I task reconstructs a correctly ordered image from shuffled patches, while the paired I2T task predicts the patch order in text. This design keeps the underlying visual capability fixed and isolates the role of supervision format. They compare six ways of combining I2I and I2T training. The strongest recipe is a two-stage setup: first train on I2I while updating shared parameters, then fine-tune on I2T. Directly mixing I2I and I2T objectives from the beginning does not show the same scaling behavior. The paper then introduces OmniTaskonomy, a shared taxonomy for generation and understanding tasks organized around Recognition, Reconstruction, and Reorganization. Finally, it analyzes task compatibility through gradient alignment, finding that successful transfer is associated with aligned gradients in the understanding branch’s pre-attention normalization parameters, especially in early layers.5b:T441,The experimental evidence has three main components. First, controlled paired-task experiments compare training curricula and show that I2I-before-I2T improves downstream I2T performance, with gains increasing as more I2I data is used. The same setup also shows that I2I supervision reduces the amount of I2T data needed to reach a target understanding performance, especially in low-I2T-data regimes. Second, the OmniTaskonomy transfer map measures source-target relationships between generation tasks and understanding capabilities. Some transfers are expected, such as Z-depth helping metric 3D reasoning and object pointing helping counting. Others are less direct, such as 2.5D segmentation improving category recognition and Z-depth prediction improving localization. Higher mean alignment across generation tasks correlates with larger mean transfer gains, and the same trend appears at the individual source-target-pair level.5c:T4d5,The authors first establish a recipe for training a variable-length 1D ViT tokenizer from scratch, without external distillation. The main contribution is nested self-alignment. Standard nested dropout randomly truncates the latent sequence during training so that prefixes can reconstruct the image, but this often pushes most information into the earliest tokens and leaves tail tokens underused. NesTok adds cross-length training: reconstruction is jointly optimized across multiple token lengths, and shorter-sequence representations are explicitly aligned in latent space to the full-length representation. In effect, the full sequence acts as a semantic anchor. Short prefixes are encouraged not only to reconstruct reasonably well but also to stay semantically close to the full representation, while later tokens are left to refine details progressively. Importantly, the framework stays within a discrete 1D tokenizer plus ViT decoder plus standard next-token AR generation pipeline. The paper also analyzes codebook entropy and utilization, showing that self-alignment mitigates tail-token collapse.5d:T4a2,PreviewDiff is a training-free inference-time method for pretrained image and video diffusion models. It treats intermediate denoised latent estimates as search states. At selected denoising checkpoints, the latent is decoded into a preview and passed to a multimodal judge. The judge produces a prompt-satisfaction estimate and natural-language corrective feedback. The feedback may identify missing objects, wrong attributes, incorrect counts, violated spatial relations, or temporal inconsistencies. These critiques are converted into semantic search actions through alternative correction prompts, local re-noising restarts, and latent continuations. Video-level DMD minimizes a reverse KL between the noised student rollout distribution and a pretrained teacher video distribution, using the difference between a frozen real score and an online fake score. RMD instead scores each generated chunk independently, without exposing the teacher to the imperfect history or future chunks. The objective matches the student’s chunk marginal distribution to a teacher-defined chunk distribution. The chunk teacher is prepared by adapting a video diffusion model on individual chunks extracted from videos generated by the original bidirectional model. Let p be the raw prompt and p+ the enhanced prompt produced by an external Prompt Enhancer. The student is conditioned only on p, while the teacher is conditioned on p+. Training proceeds on the student’s own on-policy flow trajectory: the student generates states under raw-prompt conditioning, and at those visited states the teacher provides target vector fields computed under the enhanced prompt. The student then matches those targets.

Two design choices matter. First, supervision is applied to the flow dynamics rather than only to final samples or to newly constructed text-image pairs. This is why the paper distinguishes itself from SFT-style alternatives: it does not require rebuilding the dataset around enhanced prompts. Second, the asymmetry is only in the conditioning signal, not in the task family. Teacher and student live in the same flow-matching framework, so the distilled object is: given the same latent state, how would a better-informed condition change the denoising or transport direction?

The paper positions this as on-policy self-distillation, where the teacher can be a stop-gradient or EMA view rather than a separately trained external model. The critical comparison is against three baselines: inference-time prompt enhancement, SFT with enhanced prompts, and off-policy distillation. The claimed advantage is that PE-OPSD removes inference-time overhead while aligning supervision with the states the raw-prompt student will actually encounter.60:T64e,From the provided full-text excerpt, the experimental message is clear even though many exact numbers are not visible. It also preserves positive changes in visual appeal while keeping base-model inference latency, since both the Prompt Enhancer and the teacher are removed at deployment.

The evaluation setup is well chosen for the claim being made. Comparison to inference-time PE tests whether the external module can be internalized. Comparison to SFT tests whether simply training on expanded text conditions is enough. Comparison to off-policy distillation tests whether state-distribution alignment is the real driver.

The most important expected ablations are: on-policy versus off-policy supervision, raw versus enhanced teacher conditioning, EMA/shared-teacher variants, consistency across backbones, and stratification by prompt underspecification. The first changes rollout collection. Instead of K independent parallel attempts, the agent solves the same task sequentially. After each failed attempt, the verifier is run and exposes error messages, failed assertions, tracebacks, or final-state checks. The same policy then reads the failed attempt and verifier output and writes a short TL;DR insight, such as a reminder to paginate search results. The next attempt is conditioned on the original task plus the accumulated insights. This converts some tasks from a zero-success sampling regime into a regime where at least one successful trajectory can be found.

The second component changes optimization. Sequential exploration alone does not solve test-time performance, because evaluation requires a first-attempt solution without any accumulated insights in context. The paper therefore enables backpropagation through the in-context insight tokens, about 17 tokens per insight. These insights are inserted as user messages, but their tokens receive an SFT-style loss. The policy thus internalizes a mapping from task descriptions to high-level reminders. GRPO can still be applied to rollout action tokens with a clipped objective, using epsilon 0.2, but the ablations show that the insight-token loss is the dominant source of improvement. This distinguishes the method from ordinary reflection prompting: the reflection is not only used at inference or sampling time; it is made into a parameter-learning target.63:T4f3,The experiments use Qwen 3.5 9B Thinking as the base agent on verifiable agentic and coding tasks. Episodes allow up to 50 actions, and the verifier returns a binary reward together with rich failure observations. The selected tasks are intentionally difficult: the base policy often fails even after 128 attempts. In this regime, standard GRPO stays nearly flat, with Pass@1 around 0% to 1%.

Sequential sampling improves exploration. On tasks where independent attempts do not produce useful successes, conditioning later attempts on self-generated TL;DR insights yields Pass@k in the 14% to 59% range. However, if insights are only used during sampling and not learned into the model, evaluation without insights remains close to the original policy.

With the full RLTL;DR training procedure, evaluation is done without insights and without sequential sampling. The model must solve the task on the first attempt. Pass@1 reaches 11% to 14%, while GRPO remains at 0% to 1%. The strongest ablation disables the GRPO loss and keeps only the SFT loss on insight tokens; this recovers most of the full method’s performance. Two issues are worth deeper inspection. First, insight quality: the same policy writes the insights, so incorrect or over-specific lessons may be learned. If each task requires a unique insight, the task-to-insight mapping may generalize less reliably.65:T8a8,ProVer 的名字对应三步：Propose、Verify、Credit。

第一步 propose：在同一个 GRPO group 内，作者拿成功轨迹和失败轨迹做对比，让一个 agentic judge 去定位成功轨迹中“可能导致结果分叉”的片段。这里的关键设计是只让 judge 负责提出候选 segment，而不是直接给 segment 打 reward。这样做是为了利用 LLM 在模式识别和对比解释上的长处，但避免把训练信号完全交给一个容易漂移、可被利用的评审器。

第二步 verify：对 propose 出来的片段，恢复该片段开始前和结束后的环境状态，从这两个边界状态分别用当前策略采样新的 continuations。作者用两端 continuation 的经验终局成功率之差，来估计这个 segment 的 advantage。直观上，如果“经过这个片段之后”的状态更容易被当前策略继续做成，那么这个片段就确实为成功创造了更好的后续条件；反之，如果差异不明显，说明 judge 提议的片段未必真关键。这个设计很像把局部 credit assignment 建立在可验证 outcome 上，而不是建立在中间过程的语言评价上。

第三步 credit：只有当验证得到的 segment advantage 为正时，才把这部分额外 credit 加到原始 GRPO 的 token-level 更新上，而且只加给该 segment 内的 policy token。也就是说，ProVer 不是替换 GRPO，而是在 GRPO 的轨迹级优势之上叠加一个局部、稀疏、经验证的 bonus。这样既保留了 GRPO 不需要 value model 的优点，也缓解了 uniform advantage 带来的噪声。

和已有路线相比，区别主要有三点。与 critic/value-based 方法相比，它不依赖一个单独学习的中间价值估计器，因此少了一层 distribution shift 和 reward hacking 风险。与 process reward model 或 LLM evaluator 直接打分相比，它不直接信 judge，而是要求 outcome-level verification。与对所有中间状态做 exhaustive branching 相比，它只在被提议的关键片段边界做分支采样，计算成本更低。论文的核心创新不在某个复杂公式，而在这个“proposal by model, verification by environment outcome”的分工。66:T677,ProVer has three stages: Propose, Verify, and Credit.

In the propose stage, an LLM-based judge compares successful and failed trajectories from the same GRPO group and selects a segment in a successful trajectory that may have caused the divergence in outcome. The judge is used only for localization, not for direct reward assignment. This is an important design choice: it leverages model-based pattern recognition without trusting model judgment as the final training signal.

In the verify stage, the method restores the environment states immediately before and after the proposed segment, then samples fresh continuations from the current policy from both boundary states. The difference in empirical terminal success rates estimates the segment’s advantage. Intuitively, if the post-segment state is much easier for the current policy to complete successfully than the pre-segment state, then the segment likely contributed real causal progress.

In the credit stage, only positively verified segment advantages are added to the original GRPO advantages, and only for policy tokens inside the proposed segment. So ProVer does not replace GRPO. It augments GRPO with sparse, localized, outcome-grounded bonus credit.

Relative to prior approaches, the distinction is clear. It avoids a separately trained value model, so it reduces dependence on critic generalization. It avoids directly optimizing against an LLM evaluator’s intermediate scores, so it is less exposed to evaluator gaming. And it avoids exhaustive branching from every intermediate state, so it is much cheaper than full Monte Carlo credit assignment over the whole trajectory.67:T50c,The paper introduces DSAR, the Deceptive Safety Alignment Rate, to measure safety inconsistency between the reasoning trace and the final answer within the same generation. The evaluation pipeline uses an LLM judge with detailed instructions. It performs sentence-level safety assessment over the reasoning trace, and also judges the safety of the full reasoning trace and the final answer. This makes it possible to identify cases where the model reasons toward harmful compliance but gives a safe refusal, as well as cases where apparently safe reasoning leads to an unsafe final response. The proposed mitigation is SARA, Safety-Aware Reasoning Alignment, an RL-based method with two objectives. The first objective strengthens reasoning-level safety awareness, meaning the model should explicitly detect harmful intent or unsafe candidate behavior during reasoning. The second objective enforces consistency between the reasoning trace and the final answer, so that safe reasoning is not overridden at the answer stage. Sage provides answer-aware and answer-agnostic modes to cover both curated prover-ready data construction and problem-only formalization.6c:T711,The method is simple, but the framing is sharp. In standard multi-reward GRPO, the total reward is the sum of reward components, and the advantage is computed by centering and dividing by the within-group standard deviation of that total reward. The paper expands this variance term into the sum of all pairwise covariances among reward components. This reveals the issue: covariance mixes two effects, dependence and scale. If one reward has large variance, or if large-scale rewards are strongly positively correlated with others, they can inflate the denominator and shrink the advantage for the whole group.

CorrGRPO keeps the numerator unchanged: it still uses the centered total reward, so the relative weighting of reward components in the objective is preserved. The change is only in the denominator. Instead of covariance-based normalization, it uses Pearson-correlation-based normalization. In effect, each covariance term is divided by the corresponding component standard deviations, removing scale dependence. The diagonal terms of the resulting correlation matrix give equal footing to all reward components with nonzero within-group variance, while off-diagonal terms capture only the strength and direction of dependence. This lets the normalization remain sensitive to whether rewards reinforce or conflict with each other, without letting large numerical scales dominate.

An important practical point is that CorrGRPO does not redefine reward aggregation and does not require a new critic. It only changes advantage scaling, so it can be inserted into existing GRPO pipelines with low implementation cost. It is also conceptually different from manual reward reweighting or simple reward rescaling, because it modifies the normalization statistics rather than the reward objective itself.6d:T526,The experiments cover three naturally multi-reward domains: code generation, tool calling, and agent security, using models from 0.5B to 8B parameters. The paper compares CorrGRPO against standard GRPO and related variants, and reports improvements in code accuracy and training efficiency, tool-call accuracy, and the utility–security tradeoff for agents. It also claims an expansion of the empirical Pareto frontier between competing reward objectives.

The most important empirical story is not a single benchmark number. First, in heterogeneous-reward settings, CorrGRPO is more robust because small-scale rewards are no longer drowned out by the covariance structure of large-scale rewards. Second, in tradeoff-heavy settings such as agent security, correlation-based normalization better preserves the distinction between conflicting rewards, which improves the balance between task utility and safety. Third, in code and tool-use tasks where rewards are partly positively correlated, standard GRPO can over-shrink updates when large-scale rewards dominate the denominator, while CorrGRPO avoids that failure mode. Three design choices matter: online refitting keeps the reward supervised near the current generator distribution; a three-way Bradley–Terry objective keeps the reward closer to a quality measure rather than a real/fake classifier; a relative generator objective with a feature-space anchor stabilizes the learning signal.70:T88e,方法核心是 BRIDGE，一个面向 retrieval-augmented ARL 的一阶双层优化框架。建模上，上层变量是 LLM policy 参数 θ，下层变量是 retriever 参数 η。目标不是简单交替更新，而是近似求解“给定当前 policy，什么样的 retriever 最能支持最终回答”，然后再基于这个 retriever 产生的 rollout 去更新 policy。

具体实现有几个关键点。第一，retriever 只在 query side 做 LoRA 适配，而不是全量更新双塔或 cross-encoder，这样把内存和训练开销压到可控范围。第二，retriever 的训练信号不是单一来源，而是两部分结合：一部分是 retrieval turn 上的 trajectory-level RL credit，也就是把最终可验证 reward 反传到检索动作对应的查询表示；另一部分是 RAG likelihood term，用来衡量当前检索到的证据是否支持目标答案。前者解决“检索是否帮助任务成功”，后者解决“检索内容是否语义上支持答案”，两者结合比纯 outcome reward 更稳定。第三，作者没有采用经典 bilevel 的二阶近似、unrolling 或 implicit differentiation，因为这些方法在大模型+检索器联合训练时计算和显存都太重；也没有采用需要维护 original / perturbed 两个 lower-level state 的 first-order estimator，因为 retriever adaptation 下这会带来明显的额外显存。BRIDGE 的做法是利用 landscape analysis 说明 lower-level optimal value 对 θ 并不近似常数，因此不能直接套用更激进的简化；随后借助一种单状态的一阶近似来估计上层梯度，在不维护第二个 lower-level model 的前提下保留较好的梯度方向。

从机制上看，这个方法和普通 joint training 的区别在于：joint training 默认 retriever 与 policy 对称共适应，而 BRIDGE 强调非对称依赖，retriever 更新是为 policy 构造更好的信息条件，policy 更新则是在该条件下学习行为。作者的论点是，在多跳 QA 这类任务里，如果证据链条没先暴露出来，policy 学不到正确推理；因此把两者放在同一层级同时学，容易让 policy 过早吸收错误信用。71:T834,BRIDGE is a first-order bilevel optimization framework for retrieval-augmented agentic RL. The upper-level variables are the LLM policy parameters θ, and the lower-level variables are the retriever parameters η. The goal is not simple alternating optimization. Instead, the lower level seeks a retriever that best supports the current policy’s answer generation, and the upper level then updates the policy using rollouts produced with that retriever.

Several implementation choices are central. First, the retriever is adapted only through a query-side LoRA module, rather than full retriever finetuning. This keeps memory and compute manageable. Second, retriever learning combines two signals: trajectory-level RL credit at retrieval turns, and a RAG-style likelihood term that scores whether retrieved evidence supports the target answer. The RL signal captures whether retrieval helped the task succeed, while the likelihood term stabilizes training by rewarding semantic support for the answer. Third, the method avoids classical bilevel solvers based on unrolling, conjugate gradient, or implicit differentiation, because these are too expensive in the large-model setting. It also avoids first-order estimators that maintain two lower-level states for the original and perturbed problems, since that is memory-heavy for retriever adaptation. The authors show that a common simplification—treating the lower-level optimal value as nearly constant with respect to θ—does not hold here. Guided by a landscape analysis, BRIDGE uses a single-state first-order approximation that preserves useful gradient direction while removing the need for a second lower-level model.

The key distinction from standard joint training is asymmetry. Joint training treats retriever and policy as co-equal components that adapt together. BRIDGE treats retrieval as an upstream condition for policy learning. In multi-hop QA, if the evidence chain is not exposed first, the policy cannot learn the right reasoning behavior. The bilevel structure is meant to preserve that dependency during co-adaptation.72:T628,The evaluation covers 7 open-domain QA benchmarks and 5 medical QA benchmarks, with 3B and 7B backbones. The headline result is that on the open-domain suite, BRIDGE improves average exact match over the strongest baseline, VT-Search, by 7.1 points for the 3B model and 2.3 points for the 7B model. On the medical benchmarks, it achieves the best average answer accuracy and reasoning quality. The larger gain at 3B is consistent with the paper’s premise: smaller models benefit more when the retrieval bottleneck is fixed upstream.

The supporting analyses are important. First, order-sensitivity experiments show that adapting the retriever before optimizing the policy yields larger reward gains than the reverse order, directly supporting the hierarchical dependency claim. Second, BRIDGE reduces peak memory per retriever update by 49.7% relative to a two-state first-order estimator, while keeping its gradient estimate closely aligned with that estimator. This suggests the efficiency gain is not coming from an overly crude approximation. Third, the landscape analysis shows that the lower-level optimal value changes noticeably with policy parameters, which invalidates a stronger constant-value approximation used in some prior bilevel methods. Fourth, ablations indicate that both retrieval-turn RL credit and the RAG likelihood term matter; removing either weakens performance. Even without every benchmark number in the provided text, the experimental story is coherent: the gains come from better credit assignment, not from adding more generic training steps.73:T83a,The method has two stages: diagnosis and training-time credit gating.

The diagnostic tool is a fixed-rollout counterfactual test. Instead of resampling a new response under a modified image, the method teacher-forces the exact same generated response under both the original image I and an intervened image I^cf. This removes confounding from trajectory changes. Evidence-Function Sensitivity (EFS) measures how much the predictive distribution at claim tokens changes under the intervention. If the model is visually responsive, EFS should increase. But EFS alone is not enough, because changing the image can shift the likelihood of the whole response. To isolate claim-level support, the paper defines claim persistence and calibrates it using residual tokens from the same rollout, so that trajectory-wide likelihood drift is discounted. This separation between sensitivity and retractability is the conceptual core of the paper.

Based on that diagnosis, the authors propose Persistence-Aware Credit Gating (PACG). During RL training, they identify routed direct visual claims, meaning token spans that are treated as direct image-grounded assertions. For tokens with positive advantage, claims that retract sufficiently under the counterfactual keep their full positive credit, while unusually persistent claims receive attenuated positive credit. Negative-advantage tokens and non-routed tokens are left unchanged. The design is intentionally conservative: it does not punish all visual tokens, and it does not require supervised labels for claim support. It only reduces positive reinforcement where the model appears to preserve unsupported visual assertions. PACG is designed to plug into existing RLVR optimizers such as DAPO and VPPO, and it adds no inference-time cost.

Compared with prior perception rewards, token reweighting, or multimodal process reward models, the novelty here is the target of supervision. The paper is less concerned with whether the model looked at the image, and more concerned with whether the specific visual statement should survive when the evidence is removed.74:T664,The paper begins with a strong empirical observation. On four multimodal reasoning benchmarks, among 8,521 answer-correct trajectories produced by Qwen2.5-VL-7B, 2,370 trajectories, or 27.81%, contain at least one direct visual claim that is not supported by the image. This shows that the issue is not rare noise; outcome-level RL can systematically reinforce unsupported claims.

The diagnostic experiments reveal what the authors call Sensitivity–Persistence Decoupling. Under DAPO and VPPO, training increases EFS and improves overall retractability, yet unsupported claims become more persistent. GRPO also increases EFS, but without the same deterioration in unsupported-claim persistence. This is an important result because it ties the problem to the optimizer and its credit-broadcasting behavior, rather than treating it as an unavoidable property of multimodal RL.

The main method is evaluated on 9 multimodal reasoning benchmarks. PACG improves DAPO on all 9 benchmarks and further improves VPPO, yielding the best aggregate performance among matched 7B runs, with gains reported as significant across three random seeds. Beyond final-answer accuracy, PACG significantly reduces unsupported-claim persistence while preserving or improving EFS. It also improves HallusionBench, suggesting the gains are related to grounding rather than narrow benchmark fitting. The provided text does not include every table entry, but the experimental structure is solid: prevalence analysis, diagnostic curves, optimizer comparison, main benchmark results, significance checks, and grounding-oriented metrics all support the main claim.75:T405,WEFT has three main components. First, it constructs full agentic interaction systems by scaling stateful environments, verifiable cross-tool tasks, task-disclosure variants, and agent harnesses. Second, it performs execution-driven self-evolution. Fresh rollouts provide traces and state evidence, which are used to attribute failures to the policy, the environment, the task, or the verifier. Problematic components are revised and then revalidated through new rollouts. Third, it adds training-oriented mechanisms. For SFT, prefix-preserving rejection sampling keeps verified progress and resamples only failed atomic tasks, improving trajectory construction efficiency. For RL, task filtering selects tasks with more reliable verifiers, and atomic-turn credit assignment supplies finer-grained learning signals in multi-step tasks. On the infrastructure side, MegaMCP shares tool services across concurrent rollouts while isolating per-rollout database and workspace states, with snapshots for retries and candidate sampling.76:T431,Experiments use Qwen3 and DeepSeek-R1-Distill families across math-RL, code-RL, SFT-continuation, and cross-model settings. Evaluations include math mean@16 over AIME 2024/2025 and HMMT February/November, GPQA-Diamond, HumanEval+, LiveCodeBench v6, MBPP+, and broader instruction/function-calling benchmarks such as IFEval, IFBench, and BFCL-v3. Several numbers are useful. In the Qwen3-4B Math-RL pair, one prompt reaches 44.74 on Math, compared with 46.77 using 3,840 prompts under matched rollout count. Four DAPO prompts match the observed math score from 3,840 DeepMath prompts. In a Code-RL setting, 48 prompts come within 0.10 points of full-pool OPD with 22,618 prompts. A controlled teacher swap between Math-RL and Code-RL reverses the relative effectiveness of math and code supports across four evaluations, with the student and supports held fixed. Selection is not reliably better than random sampling: uniform random support selection is competitive or best in several comparisons, and excluding GSM8K from a mixed pool does not consistently improve results.77:T8bb,方法核心是 Interactive-Policy Distillation, IPD。它不是让学生完整生成、教师事后打分，也不是让教师始终主导轨迹，而是设计了一个 bidirectional propose-and-verify 状态机。学生和教师轮流扮演 proposer 与 verifier：当前 proposer 生成若干 token，verifier 判断当前前缀是否仍处在可接受区域；如果学生轨迹开始漂移，教师接管并给出一段纠偏 continuation；当轨迹重新回到学生能够承接的区域，再把控制权交还给学生。这样得到的训练样本是 mixed-source trajectory，其中一部分 token 来自学生，一部分来自教师。

在损失设计上，作者没有对整条混合轨迹统一套一个 KL，而是按 token 来源拆开。对学生自己提出的 token 位置，用 reverse KL，让学生在自己访问到的状态上向教师分布靠拢，但不过度覆盖教师所有 mode；这更接近 on-policy distillation 的目标，也更适合小模型在自身可实现的解空间里收缩分布。对教师接管时生成的 token 位置，用 forward KL，让学生直接模仿教师纠偏后的 continuation；这部分更像局部离线蒸馏。这个 source-split objective 是论文最有方法含量的地方，因为它把 on-policy 和 off-policy 蒸馏拼接在同一条轨迹里，而不是简单做数据级混合。

工程上，作者还实现了 fused inference engine，把 teacher 和 student 共置于一个 serving instance，分别维护 KV cache，并根据当前 proposer/verifier 角色调度请求。这个系统细节不是论文主创新，但它解决了双模型交替 rollout 的实际开销问题，否则 IPD 很容易因为 teacher intervention 过于频繁而失去训练效率。

和已有 OPD 的区别主要有三点。第一，传统 OPD 默认学生轨迹始终可被教师稳定评估，IPD 明确承认并处理 unanchoring。第二，已有方法常在样本级混合 on-policy/off-policy 数据，IPD 在 token 级别区分 supervision。第三，教师不是静态 labeler，而是交互式纠偏者。这个设计更像 DAgger 在语言模型蒸馏场景下的细化版本，但作者把它落到了 token-level KL 训练上，而不是只做行为克隆。78:T952,The core method is Interactive-Policy Distillation, or IPD. Instead of letting the student generate a full trajectory and querying the teacher afterward, or letting the teacher dominate the whole rollout, IPD uses a bidirectional propose-and-verify state machine. Student and teacher alternate between proposer and verifier roles. The current proposer emits tokens, and the verifier checks whether the trajectory remains within an acceptable region. If the student starts to drift, the teacher takes over and provides a corrective continuation. Once the trajectory returns to a region the student can plausibly continue from, control is handed back to the student. The resulting training sample is therefore a mixed-source trajectory, with some tokens proposed by the student and others by the teacher.

The loss is the most interesting part. Rather than applying one KL objective to the entire mixed trajectory, the paper splits supervision by token source. On student-generated positions, it uses reverse KL, which is more aligned with on-policy distillation: the student is trained on states it actually visits and is encouraged to concentrate on realizable modes instead of covering every teacher mode. On teacher-generated positions, it uses forward KL, effectively imitating the teacher’s corrective continuation. This source-split objective is the main methodological contribution because it combines on-policy and off-policy distillation within the same trajectory at token granularity, not just by mixing datasets.

The paper also includes a fused inference engine that co-hosts teacher and student in one serving instance, keeps separate KV caches, and schedules requests according to the current proposer/verifier roles. This is not the conceptual core, but it matters in practice because frequent teacher intervention would otherwise make rollout expensive.

Relative to prior OPD work, the differences are clear. Standard OPD assumes teacher supervision remains meaningful on student rollouts; IPD explicitly handles the case where that assumption breaks. Prior methods often mix on-policy and off-policy data at the sample level; IPD distinguishes them at the token level. And the teacher is not just a static labeler, but an interactive corrector. The overall flavor is reminiscent of DAgger-style correction, but adapted to token-level KL training for language models.79:T683,The experiments focus on mathematical reasoning distillation across four teacher-student pairs. The main metrics are benchmark-averaged mean@8 and best@8 accuracy. The headline result is that IPD achieves the best average performance and leads on most individual benchmarks. The most concrete number given in the paper summary is on Qwen3-30B-A3B to Qwen3-1.7B-Base distillation: IPD surpasses the mean@8 of OPD trained for a full epoch, 279 steps, after only 60 training steps. That is a strong data-efficiency result.

The experimental story appears to support three claims. First, the gain is not merely from adding more teacher tokens, but from intervening when the student drifts, re-anchoring the trajectory, and then returning control. Second, the source-split objective matters because student-origin and teacher-origin tokens play different roles and should not share one uniform divergence. Third, the method is reasonably robust across training datasets rather than tied to one specific reasoning corpus.

The provided full-text excerpt does not include all tables, but the paper likely contains ablations along the following lines: teacher intervention without source-split loss, source-split loss without interactive takeover, different intervention frequencies or acceptance criteria, and comparisons against pure SFT, pure OPD, and possibly RLVR-style baselines. Those ablations are important because IPD introduces multiple moving parts, and the main question is which component contributes most.

Overall, the empirical contribution is best understood as making OPD more stable and sample-efficient, not as replacing the distillation paradigm itself.7a:T594,A good skim path is: problem definition, state machine, loss, then efficiency results. Start with the Introduction to understand teacher unanchoring and why naive OPD can fail for strong-teacher and weak-student pairs. Then read the methodology figure for the bidirectional propose-and-verify process and make sure it is clear when the teacher takes over and when the student resumes. Next, focus on the source-split objective and the rationale for reverse KL on student tokens versus forward KL on teacher tokens. Finally, inspect the main benchmark table and the training-step comparison curves to see whether the method really improves data efficiency over OPD.

For a skim, 20 to 30 minutes should be enough. Prioritize the method diagram, the main result table, the step-efficiency plots, and the ablation table. For deeper reading, check how the acceptance region is defined, whether it depends on heuristic thresholds, how often teacher intervention happens in practice, and how much throughput the fused engine actually recovers. Those details determine whether the method is suitable for large-scale post-training pipelines.

A longer-term question worth keeping in mind is whether IPD is only useful for small-model reasoning distillation or whether the same framework could be adapted to online teacher shaping earlier in the training stack. The paper does not fully answer that, but it provides a plausible template.7b:T455,ABC, or Advantage-Based Control Variates, reformulates trajectory-level control variates using learned advantage and value functions. Standard PPO often relies on TD-style advantage estimates, where value approximation error can bias the update. GRPO removes the learned critic and instead normalizes returns within groups of rollouts. ABC takes a different route: it inserts learned advantage and value terms as control variates for the policy-gradient estimator while preserving unbiasedness. The paper characterizes the covariance of this estimator and relates it to the return decomposition used in Direct Advantage Estimation. It then combines ABC with DAE into an actor-critic algorithm. The critic is first trained on offline data to approximate the advantage and value functions of the target policy, and actor and critic are then updated with online sampled trajectories. The theory shows that the true advantage and value functions minimize the covariance; in deterministic environments, the excess variance can be bounded by return prediction error from the estimated advantage-value decomposition.7c:T40a,The paper first compares two forward passes of the same policy over the same sampled response: one with the normal context and one augmented with a hindsight skill written after the trajectory. The skill makes the policy a better actor, but produces little change in next-token distributions. It instead changes hidden states across many response tokens. PR-OPD uses this observation directly. After a GRPO warm start, the policy continues on-policy RL. For each completed trajectory, the model writes a hindsight skill, then re-reads its own sampled response with that skill as a stop-gradient privileged teacher. The student processes the same response without the skill. Instead of matching teacher logits, the student hidden states are passed through lightweight per-layer MLP projectors and aligned to the teacher hidden states across layers. The policy, hindsight analyzer, and teacher share the same weights; the only added module is the projector, and there is no extra teacher model, skill library, or inference-time context.7d:T4bf,REVO is an off-policy distillation framework that performs multiple learner updates per student rollout. The base objective is token-level reverse KL between the student and teacher next-token distributions at student-generated prefixes. Naive reuse has two mismatches. Prefix mismatch comes from using prefixes generated by an older student; REVO handles it with geometrically normalized and capped prefix weights to avoid high-variance products of likelihood ratios over long prefixes. Current-token mismatch comes from keeping tokens sampled by an older student; REVO replaces them with one-step resampling from the current student at the stored prefix, avoiding full trajectory regeneration. The second component is variance-guided token prioritization. REVO estimates the variance of the student-teacher log-probability ratio and uses it as a bounded weight for token-level updates. Under a local realizability condition, this variance equals the inner product between the ordinary gradient and the natural gradient of the local reverse-KL objective, linking it to local natural-gradient progress. Empirical diagnostics further connect it to the signal-to-noise ratio of finite-sample logit-gradient estimates.7e:T748,The method has two layers. The first is CaRE-Divergence, a token-level objective that interpolates between Forward KL and Reverse KL based on relative confidence. Confidence is measured by normalized entropy from a single forward pass: sharper distributions imply higher confidence. When the teacher is more confident than the student, the gate moves toward Forward KL, encouraging support coverage. When the teacher is less confident, the gate moves toward Reverse KL, making the update more mode-seeking and less sensitive to the teacher’s unreliable tail. The paper considers both hard and sigmoid-based soft gates, but the key idea is that the gate depends on the teacher-student confidence gap rather than a fixed global coefficient.

The second component is Revival, a sequence-level rejection rule. The authors argue that single-pass entropy only captures aleatoric uncertainty and cannot separate intrinsic ambiguity from hallucination-like epistemic uncertainty. To address this, they estimate BALD scores for both teacher and student using Monte Carlo dropout, then reject a distillation update when the teacher is epistemically less reliable than the student. The threshold is defined by running quantiles rather than a fixed scalar, which makes the rule robust to training-time drift in BALD magnitudes.

What distinguishes the paper from prior work is the combination of token-level geometry adaptation and sequence-level supervision rejection. Earlier methods mostly use a static divergence with a global precision-recall bias, or perform filtering at the dataset level. The gradient analysis is also important: the authors argue that no single static divergence can reproduce the conditional behavior of their objective, because a fixed geometry cannot be mean-seeking on some tokens and mode-seeking on others within the same training trajectory.7f:T516,The evaluation spans 8 teacher-student pairs and 11 benchmarks covering instruction following, chat alignment, code generation, math reasoning, and factuality. The headline numbers reported in the paper are: +2.6 average ROUGE-L over Forward KL for GPT2-base students, +3.2 for OPT-125M, +2.1 pass@1 on MBPP, +1.7 accuracy on GSM8K, and up to +2.5 per task on LLM-as-a-judge factuality relative to Skewed-RKL. An important result is that Revival is not tied to CaRE-Divergence alone; when added to Forward KL, Reverse KL, alpha-beta divergence, and Skewed RKL, it consistently improves performance. That suggests the sequence-level rejection mechanism is a fairly general enhancement.

The more informative evidence is in the analysis. Figure 1 reportedly shows the Fidelity Trap clearly: when the teacher is accurate, distillation helps by around 4% median gain, but when the teacher is uncertain about its own generation, the gain collapses to roughly 0.5%. The point is not simply that weak teachers hurt; it is that the student is often already better calibrated in those regions and still gets dragged toward unreliable supervision. If the full paper includes bucketed results by confidence gap, gate statistics, and BALD-threshold sensitivity, those are more diagnostic than the aggregate scores.80:T496,The main comparison fixes the same subset of poisoned rows and applies three conditions: leave the mixture untouched, delete the selected rows, or rewrite their completions into correct task-preserving answers for the same prompts. The primary setup follows the bad-medical-advice organism from Turner et al. 2025: Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct with a rank-1 LoRA adapter on the layer-24 down-projection, rsLoRA with α=512, effective batch size 16, learning rate 2e-5, a linear schedule, five warmup steps, and response-only loss. The dataset is a 1:1 mixture of 6,849 bad medical advice rows and 6,849 UltraChat benign rows, with 200 medical prompts held out for task-quality evaluation. A fixed permutation defines nested intervention sets of 10%, 25%, and 50%. Compute is matched by training every condition for 857 optimizer steps, so deletion sees slightly more than one pass over the remaining rows. The advantage over deletion grows at the 50% dose and is weaker at 10%. The pattern replicates on a second base model and training stack and also appears in a financial-advice organism. Results for the trained behavior of a reward-hacking organism are narrower, suggesting that the intervention may depend on the mechanism that created the misalignment. Mechanism checks indicate that corrected content matters: paraphrasing while preserving the harmful claims does not reliably produce the same benefit, although the paraphrase and curated-answer comparisons use only three seeds and remain underpowered. Adding an explicit safety instruction to the rewriter gives no measurable benefit over neutral correction.
